extracted.intended_audience: researchers, academics, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions (particularly in mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: News-style summaries and case reports about retractions, withdrawals, corrections, and editorial fallout in mathematics publications, describing reasons and process. The page aggregates individual posts about specific incidents and the factual/contextual details behind each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors invalidating main results (correctness/validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the paper contains errors which invalidate its main results."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases where outside experts identify mathematical or methodological errors that undermine the central claims, prompting retraction. Example: Manuscripta Mathematica retracted a 2015 paper after experts said errors invalidated main results. Guidance implied: if errors fundamentally invalidate conclusions, retraction is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / originality (results must be new)
rubrics_metrics.description: The results must be new; papers may be withdrawn if results are 'already known' or duplicate existing definitions/results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Communications in Algebra withdrew a paper after discovering the same property had already been defined (author was unaware). Editors framed this as 'definitely not a matter of plagiarism' but still grounds for withdrawal because the contribution lacked novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and failure to credit prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must properly credit prior work; an author's 'failure to credit Beer’s work' was cited in a correction over alleged plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantial overlap or unattributed use of another's work is identified, issues range from correction notices to resignations and potential retractions depending on severity. Example: Scientific Reports issued a correction citing errors and failure to credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper ethical approvals and clear reporting of approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: "NTU believes [the paper] did not receive proper ethical approvals" — lack of clear ethical approval can trigger investigation and retraction activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should obtain and clearly state required ethical approvals; ambiguous or missing approvals can lead institutions or journals to request retraction or to investigate, and may prompt administrative actions (e.g., contract termination) while inquiries proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate remedial action: retraction vs correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the issue merits a correction notice or a retraction (e.g., journal issued a correction but affected parties felt that wasn't sufficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scale and nature of the problem (degree to which results are undermined, plagiarism, ethical breaches) determine whether a correction suffices or a full retraction is necessary. Stakeholders may disagree on adequacy of correction versus retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial process and oversight (consultation with editorial board)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance decisions should follow journal governance; acceptance 'was a serious mistake' when made without consulting the editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals are expected to follow established editorial procedures and to consult editorial boards for significant decisions; failure to do so can lead to public criticism and resignations by editors-in-chief who 'assumed responsibility for these mistakes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and disclosure (sharing underlying documentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency in disputes is important — e.g., 'Surface those emails' to allow inspection of communications supporting claims about what happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing underlying emails, statements, and supporting documents can help clarify the sequence of events and reasons for editorial decisions or retractions, and is used by journalists and stakeholders to inform the public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing inaccurate results from misconduct (fraud vs error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language matters: editors clarified that phrase 'most results are false' meant findings were inaccurate, 'not fraudulent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When results are wrong, determining whether the cause is honest error or intentional fraud affects how cases are framed, institutions respond, and reputations are affected. Notices should ideally distinguish inaccuracy from misconduct where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and latency of retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions can occur long after publication — e.g., 'why did it occur 16 years after the paper was published?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and the community should consider that problems may surface many years later; the timeliness of investigation and retraction influences community trust and the utility of the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant publication / notice of redundant publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers may be withdrawn for redundant publication when results duplicate prior work (not necessarily plagiarism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redundancy (publishing known results under a new label) can warrant withdrawal or notice of redundant publication; journals may characterize such situations as error rather than misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate channel and provenance for retraction statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions/corrections should be issued via proper channels; one author retracted conference proceedings on his personal blog after discovering errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the standard is journal or conference proceedings issuing formal notices, in some cases authors publicly announce withdrawals via blogs or preprint servers; best practice is for formal archival notice in the venue of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability measures beyond retraction (resignations, contract termination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences for problematic publications can include editorial resignations and institutional actions like contract termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional investigations can lead to employment consequences separate from publication notices; editorial resignations are sometimes used to signal responsibility for editorial mistakes.
